examDifficulty.heading: Is the Heroku Developer Accredited Professional Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: It is a practical exam about building and running apps on Heroku. If you have deployed real apps, most topics will be familiar. The tricky parts are Heroku-specific details like release phase, dyno behaviour and Heroku Connect.
bullets: 68% to pass, which is 41 correct answers.
Platform details. Dyno types, the Procfile, buildpacks, config vars and add-ons all come up.
Salesforce link. Expect questions on Heroku Connect and calling Salesforce from a Heroku app.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Deploy a small app with a database, a worker and Heroku Connect before the exam. Before you book, aim for 75% or more on practice tests.

examFormat.heading: Heroku Developer Accredited Professional Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: Accredited Professional exams are taken online. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions describe a developer task, such as running a migration, adding a background job or fixing a failing deploy, and ask for the right Heroku feature or command.
bestWayToPass: Know the Procfile: How web, worker and release process types are defined.
Keep config out of code: Config vars hold settings and secrets, and add-ons set their own config vars.
Learn Heroku Connect: How it maps Salesforce objects to Postgres tables, and read-only versus read-write sync.
Use logs and metrics: Know heroku logs, log drains and the main error codes.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you build, deploy and run apps on Heroku: dynos, buildpacks, config vars, add-ons, background jobs, logging and Heroku Connect.

keyConcepts.h2: Heroku Developer AP: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Buildpacks, Runtime & Procfile
blocks.body: When you push code, Heroku uses a **buildpack** to detect the language and build it into a **slug**, or builds a Docker image if you use container deploys. The **Procfile** in the root of the app says which commands to run: `web` for the process that takes HTTP traffic and must listen on the port in the PORT variable, `worker` for background jobs, and `release` for tasks that run before each new release goes live, such as database migrations. If a release command fails, the new release isn't deployed.

blocks.heading: Config Vars, Add-ons & Environment Management
blocks.body: **Config vars** are environment variables for settings and secrets, so the same code runs in every environment. Changing a config var restarts the app with the new value. **Add-ons** are managed services such as Heroku Postgres, Key-Value Store, logging or monitoring tools. When you add one, it sets config vars like DATABASE_URL for you. Use separate apps for staging and production, grouped in a **pipeline**, each with its own config vars and add-ons.

blocks.heading: Heroku Connect & Salesforce Integration
blocks.body: **Heroku Connect** syncs Salesforce objects with tables in Heroku Postgres. You choose the objects and fields to map. **Read-only** mappings copy Salesforce changes into Postgres. **Read-write** mappings also send Postgres changes back to Salesforce. This lets a Heroku app read and write Salesforce data with plain SQL, without using API calls in the app. Sync isn't instant, so apps must allow a short delay. For direct, real-time work, a Heroku app can also call the Salesforce REST API using OAuth.

blocks.heading: Async Jobs, Workers & Message Queues
blocks.body: Web requests that take longer than 30 seconds are cut off by the router, so slow work belongs on a **worker dyno**. The web dyno puts a job on a queue, often in Heroku Key-Value Store, and the worker picks it up. Scheduled tasks can run with **Heroku Scheduler**, which starts a one-off dyno at set times. For high-volume event streams between services, **Apache Kafka on Heroku** is an option. Workers should be safe to retry, because a dyno restart can stop a job halfway.

blocks.heading: Monitoring, Logging & Performance
blocks.body: Heroku collects logs from the router, dynos and add-ons into one stream, called **Logplex**. View them with `heroku logs --tail`, or send them to an outside tool with a **log drain**. Error codes tell you what went wrong: for example, H10 means the app crashed and H12 means a request timed out. **Metrics** show response time, memory and load. Scale **horizontally** by adding dynos, or **vertically** with bigger dyno types. Memory errors (R14) usually mean the dyno type is too small or the app is leaking memory.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Heroku Developer Accredited Professional Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions are everyday developer tasks on Heroku. Pick the Heroku-native way to do it.

blocks.heading: Heroku Deployment Workflow
blocks.body: Push to Git or connect GitHub, use review apps for pull requests, and promote builds through a pipeline from staging to production.

blocks.heading: Dyno Configuration & Scaling
blocks.body: Web for HTTP, worker for background jobs, one-off for admin tasks. Scale out with more dynos or up with bigger types.

blocks.heading: Heroku Postgres
blocks.body: Use followers for read-heavy work, forks for testing, and backups before risky changes. Run migrations in release phase.

blocks.heading: Heroku Connect Setup
blocks.body: Read-only to copy Salesforce data into Postgres. Read-write to also send changes back. Allow for a short sync delay.

blocks.heading: Config Vars & Add-ons
blocks.body: Settings and secrets go in config vars. Add-ons set their own config vars, like DATABASE_URL.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Certifications After This AP
nextCertsAfter.intro: Good next steps after Heroku Developer:

sampleQuestions.question: Database migrations must run each time a new version is deployed, before the new code takes traffic. Where should the migration command go?
options: A worker dyno that runs forever
sampleQuestions.explanation: The release process runs after the build and before the new release goes live. If it fails, the release is stopped.
whyWrong: A worker isn't tied to the release timing.
A README doesn't run anything.
Running migrations in the web process can cause errors while dynos start.

sampleQuestions.question: A web process starts but Heroku reports error H10, and the app crashes on boot. The app listens on port 3000. What is the likely cause?
options: The app must listen on the PORT variable
The app needs a bigger dyno
sampleQuestions.explanation: Heroku assigns the port at run time through the PORT variable. An app that listens on a fixed port can't receive traffic.
whyWrong: A full database causes different errors.
Dyno size doesn't affect which port the app uses.
Buildpack version isn't the issue here.

sampleQuestions.question: Where should an app's API keys and database URL be stored on Heroku?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Config vars keep settings and secrets out of the code, and each app or environment has its own values.
whyWrong: A public folder can be downloaded by anyone.
The Procfile lists commands, not secrets.
Secrets in code end up in Git history.

sampleQuestions.question: A request that sends 5,000 emails takes over a minute, and users see H12 timeout errors. What should the developer do?
options: Queue the job and use a worker dyno
sampleQuestions.explanation: The router stops requests after 30 seconds. Long jobs should run on a worker dyno in the background.
whyWrong: A larger dyno may still take more than 30 seconds.
The router timeout can't be raised.
The router cuts the request no matter how long users wait.

sampleQuestions.question: A Heroku app needs to read Salesforce Contact data with fast SQL queries, without using Salesforce API calls on every request. What should be used?
options: A REST API call on every request
A CSV file uploaded each week
sampleQuestions.explanation: Heroku Connect copies Salesforce records into Postgres, so the app can query them with SQL.
whyWrong: API calls on every request are slower and use up limits.
Config vars are for settings, not records.
A weekly file goes out of date.

sampleQuestions.question: Users update their contact details in a Heroku app, and the changes must flow back to Salesforce. What mapping type is needed?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Read-write mappings send changes made in Postgres back to Salesforce.
whyWrong: Log drains send logs, not data.
Followers are read copies of a database.
Read-only mappings only copy data from Salesforce.

sampleQuestions.question: A cleanup task must run every night at 2 a.m. What is the simplest option?
options: Running the task by hand every single night
Heroku Scheduler running a one-off dyno
A web dyno that sleeps until 2 a.m.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Heroku Scheduler starts a one-off dyno on a schedule to run the task.
whyWrong: Release phase runs only on deploys.
Manual work is easy to forget.
A sleeping web dyno is wasteful and restarts can lose the timer.

sampleQuestions.question: The team wants all app logs sent to an outside logging service for search and alerts. What should they set up?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Log drains forward the app's log stream to an outside service.
whyWrong: Review apps are for testing pull requests.
Followers copy database data.
Dyno size doesn't affect where logs go.

sampleQuestions.question: Metrics show frequent R14 errors on a web dyno. What do they mean?
options: The dyno has exceeded its memory limit
sampleQuestions.explanation: R14 means memory quota exceeded. The fix is to reduce memory use or move to a larger dyno type.
whyWrong: A boot crash is H10.
Database problems show different errors.
A request timeout is H12.

sampleQuestions.question: After adding Heroku Postgres to an app, how does the app find the database?
options: The developer types the password into the code
The add-on sets the DATABASE_URL config var
The app scans the network for databases
sampleQuestions.explanation: Add-ons set config vars automatically. The app reads DATABASE_URL to connect.
whyWrong: Typing secrets into code is unsafe and unnecessary.
Apps don't need to search for the database.
Heroku doesn't send connection details by email.

sampleQuestions.question: A tested build in staging should go to production exactly as it is. How should it be done?
options: Push the code again to production
Rebuild it with a new buildpack
sampleQuestions.explanation: Promotion copies the same slug to production, so what was tested is what goes live.
whyWrong: Pushing again creates a new build that might differ.
A new buildpack produces a different build.
Heroku doesn't deploy by FTP.

sampleQuestions.question: A background worker is restarted halfway through a job. What should the developer design for?
options: Jobs that can never be interrupted
Running all jobs in the web dyno
Jobs that can be retried without duplicate effects
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dynos restart regularly, so jobs should be safe to run again, for example by checking whether the work is already done.
whyWrong: No job can be guaranteed to finish without interruption.
Web dynos have the 30-second limit and the same restarts.
You can't turn off the daily restart.

sampleQuestions.question: A Heroku app needs to create Salesforce Cases in real time when a user submits a form. Heroku Connect isn't set up. What should it do?
options: Write it to a local file and then email it
Call the Salesforce REST API using OAuth
sampleQuestions.explanation: The REST API lets the app create records straight away, using an OAuth token for access.
whyWrong: Chatter posts aren't Cases.
A local file is lost on restart and isn't an integration.
A nightly batch isn't real time.

sampleQuestions.question: Traffic doubles during a sale and response times rise. The app is stateless. What is the quickest fix?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Stateless apps scale out easily: more web dynos share the extra traffic.
whyWrong: Logging has little effect on response time.
Removing the database breaks the app.
Restarts don't add capacity.

sampleQuestions.question: The team wants a temporary app created for every GitHub pull request so reviewers can test it. What should they use?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Review apps create a short-lived app per pull request and remove it when the pull request closes.
whyWrong: Scheduler runs tasks on a timer.
One-off dynos run single commands.
A second production app isn't tied to pull requests.
